column2: FIS is Dr. Bardia Khosravani’s investing system: find good companies with Codal reports, not with charts.
In his research paper, FIS gives each company a score from 0 to 100 on 11 measures.
The goals he names: lasting profit with low risk, income without daily work, and retiring earlier. These are goals, not guarantees.
Like buying a rental property: you want one that pays reliable rent every month, not one that might get expensive some day.
There are two kinds of share. “Dividend-focused”: pays most of its profit to shareholders in cash every year.
“Growth-focused”: keeps profit and spends it on new projects; the shareholder’s gain comes more from the price going up.
Where is the line? He has confirmed that a company paying out more than 60% of its profit is dividend-focused; and for “good” he uses above 70% as the benchmark.
In Iran, FIS prefers the first kind.
Think of an orchard: one sells the fruit every year and gives you the money; the other plants the fruit so the orchard grows bigger.
According to him classic theories don’t work well in Iran, because sanctions, the dollar, government decisions and war shake the whole market together.
A dividend is money that has reached you and is no longer exposed to these risks.
When a company pays dividends year after year, it proves its profit is real, not just on paper.
This money can be invested again or spent on living.
A tenant who pays rent on time every month is better than one who promises to pay it all at the end of the year.
This section comes from Dr. Khosravani’s public teachings: his blog, research paper, videos and Telegram channel, in this app’s own words.
It doesn’t rewrite his paid courses.
His return claims, like “a return of twice inflation”, are only quoted here, not tested.
Like the notes a student writes from a professor’s public lectures; their private class is something else.
A good share in FIS meets three conditions:
1. It makes lasting profit every year.
2. It pays a large part of its profit to shareholders in cash.
3. Its profit grows faster than inflation, so the dividend really gets bigger each year.
A good rental property: always has a tenant (lasting profit), the rent reaches you (high payout), and the rent rises faster than inflation each year (growth).
The three golden conditions
Compare profit growth with inflation, not with zero.
Profit went from 1,000 to 1,400 (40%) and inflation was 30%: real growth is about 7.7%; the third condition is met.
If profit goes up 25% but inflation is 35%, profit actually got smaller.
Measure the average of several years, not one very good year.
If rent goes up 25% but everything gets 35% dearer, this year’s rent buys less than last year’s.
Lasting profit: 5 years of operating profit in the annual reports, and the monthly reports for this year.
High payout: the dividend per share (DPS) in the meeting minutes, and its ratio to earnings per share over several years.
Growth above inflation: put several years of earnings per share and dividends next to those years’ inflation.
A high dividend paid with a loan is a warning bell, not a golden condition.
Like checking a tenant: several years of payment history, rent receipts, and whether they pay the rent from their own pocket or borrow it.
Dividend yield = dividend per share ÷ share price.
A price of 5,000 and a dividend of 1,000 rials means a 20% dividend yield.
If the company pays out the same share of its profit every year, approximate total return = dividend yield + profit growth.
A house worth 1 billion that brings 200 million a year in rent has a 20% rental yield.
On the day the ticker reopens after the meeting, the price drops by the amount of that dividend; money moved from one of your pockets to the other.
Payment is due within 8 months at most, and small shareholders usually get it sooner.
According to him, if next year’s profit is bigger, the price goes back up; so the price recovering depends on profit growth, not on the meeting itself.
If you take 20,000 tomans out of a piggy bank holding 100,000, you have 20,000 in your pocket and the piggy bank has 80,000; your total is the same.
He puts a share’s return next to bank interest, bonds and property rent. Rates change every year; compare with today’s rates.
The danger with deposits and bonds: inflation beats their return.
The danger with property: it’s slow to sell and costs money to keep up.
The danger with shares: price falls, whole-market risk, and falling profit.
Before you put your money somewhere, you ask: how much reaches me each year, and does it keep up with rising prices?
Comparing with banks, bonds and rent
Sometimes a share’s price comes down while the company’s profit and dividend go up; so the dividend yield gets bigger.
Dr. Khosravani calls this price drop a “golden buying opportunity”.
But only when the three golden conditions still hold and the buying was planned in advance. Sometimes a price drop shows news that isn’t in the reports yet.
If the price of a house whose rent has gone up falls because of general fear, it’s an opportunity; unless someone knows a motorway is about to be built next to it.
Low price, high profit
When the dividends you’ve received add up to what you paid for the share, your money has come back and the share you still own is in effect “free”.
Example: 10 million tomans of a share with a 25% dividend yield and dividend growth of 30% a year: 2.5, then 3.25, then 4.23 million; about 3 years.
The goal he gives: getting your money back from dividends in about 3 years. It isn’t possible with every share.
“Free” is an accounting idea: 10 million three years later, with inflation, buys less.
If you buy a car and earn back its price driving passengers in 3 years, the car you still have has in effect become free for you.
The free share
How much capital is needed for dividends to cover your living costs? Monthly spending × 12 ÷ dividend yield.
With monthly spending of 40 million and a 20% dividend yield: 40 × 12 ÷ 0.2 = 2.4 billion tomans.
Spending rises with inflation every year; so dividends must also grow at least as fast as inflation.
Dividends arrive once a year, sometimes late; so rainy-day money and a monthly plan are needed.
Like wanting to live off the rent of a few flats: you need to know how many flats it takes for the rents to cover the year’s costs.
He tells the story of someone who, from 1396, every month first bought a few shares of a dividend-focused company with his salary, and then spent the rest.
The habit matters more than the amount: regular monthly buying, holding, and meeting dividends adding up.
Remember the examples that get told are hand-picked; there were also shares that never became free.
Like someone who buys a small gold coin at the start of every month and then spends; after a few years they’re surprised how much has added up.
He sees his own retirement at 28 as the result of collecting meeting dividends and holding shares.
The biggest mistake he tells of himself: he pulled money out of the market to buy a physical asset; that is, he switched off the profit-making machine.
“Enjoying is different from owning”: to enjoy a villa you don’t need to lock your money in a villa.
These are his personal experiences; weigh them against your own situation.
Renting a villa for a week’s holiday is much cheaper than buying a villa you use one week a year.
He gives the goal of the Master FIS course as financial independence in 5 to 7 years.
This is a goal, not a guarantee; it depends on how much you save, the real return and inflation.
Work it out yourself: write down your yearly spending and see how many years it takes with your savings and your real dividend yield.
Like a plan to buy a home: if you save 10 million a month and the home costs 2 billion, simple maths says how many years it takes, and inflation makes it longer.
On his channel (Khordad 1403) he wrote out Sorood’s numbers: the whole company’s value at the start of 1399 was about 840 billion tomans.
Over the next 3 years its dividends added up to 832 billion tomans; so almost all the purchase money came back from dividends alone.
His other example is Fazar: 74% of the purchase money in 3 years.
Remember this is a nominal return; 832 billion three years later, with inflation, isn’t worth the 840 billion of the day of purchase.
Like a shop you bought for 840 million that brought 832 million in rent over 3 years; your money is almost back and the shop is still yours.
A real example: Sorood
When a company raises capital with shareholders’ fresh money, for each share you have the right to buy one new share for 1,000 rials. This right is called a “right” (haqq-e taqaddom).
A right’s ticker is usually the share’s ticker with an “H” at the end.
Within the deadline (usually 60 days) you either pay the 1,000 rials and get the share, or sell the right on the market.
If you do neither, it’s sold for you and the money usually arrives later and sometimes for less.
Like first claim to buy a new flat in a building where you already own one: either you buy at a low price, or you sell this right to someone else.
What is a right?
A right is worth roughly: share price − 1,000 rials; because by paying 1,000 rials you get the same share.
The example from his blog: a share at 6,000 rials and 3 new shares for each share. The price after the increase: (6,000 + 3 × 1,000) ÷ 4 = 2,250; the right is about 1,250.
The wealth of someone who pays doesn’t change: 100 shares × 6,000 + 300 thousand paid = 400 shares × 2,250.
If a concert ticket is worth 500 thousand tomans and you have the right to buy it for 100 thousand, that right itself is worth about 400 thousand.
If the old share gets the coming meeting’s dividend but the new share doesn’t, the right is worth less.
Example: share 4,000 and a coming dividend of 500. Fair right ≈ 4,000 − 500 − 1,000 = 2,500. If it trades at 3,000, it’s about 500 rials too expensive.
Which year’s profit the new share gets is stated in the notice and the meeting minutes on Codal.
The 1,000 rials you pay months in advance also earns nothing in that time.
If a house is sold with its tenant but this year’s rent stays with the seller, the buyer should pay less.
The expensive right
From his note: a company’s net profit must give a return in line with the current value of its shares (market value), not the old book number.
And this return must fit the risk.
His example: market value 1,000 billion tomans and a required return of 30%, so at least 300 billion of profit. Less than that means the company is destroying wealth.
According to him many companies on Iran’s exchange don’t meet this condition.
If a house is worth 10 billion and brings only 200 million a year in rent, even though it makes money, you’ve tied up your money badly.
Each industry has its own usual profit margin.
Don’t compare a 30% net margin in steel with a distributor’s 3 to 4%.
Judge each company’s margin against its own industry’s average and its own past years.
A supermarket makes a little on each item but sells a lot; a jeweller makes a lot on each item but sells little. Both can be good.
Market value = price × number of shares; that is, the price of the whole company.
Small companies: more risk, harder to buy and sell, sometimes more growth.
Large companies (holdings, banks, refineries, petrochemicals): usually less risk.
A big supermarket chain is different from a small corner shop: the first is steadier, the second may grow faster or close sooner.
Small, medium and large companies
For the long term he sees large industries such as refining, copper, steel, iron ore and petrochemical holdings as a lower-risk path to growth.
Their profit goes up and down with world prices and the dollar; so price them on several years’ average profit.
Lower risk doesn’t mean no risk; the three golden conditions and buying cheap are still needed.
A wheat farmer has rainy years and dry years; it’s good land, but they work out their income on the average of several years.
The analyses he writes tagged FIS have these parts:
Industry and product; who sets the product and raw-material prices; the main owner and the percentage of free-floating shares.
The return of past years (price growth + dividends); past and forward P/E; the forecast assumptions, written down.
What happens if the most important assumption changes; and the last sentence: “This is analysis, not a buy recommendation.”
Like a car inspection report: specs, history, price, assumptions, and at the end “this is an expert opinion; the decision is yours”.
Write assumptions out plainly; for example: production = the average of the last 2 years, sales = production, prices = the latest traded price.
In one of his analyses: market value 2,850 and forecast profit 650 billion tomans, so a forward P/E of about 4.4.
Then work out profit with production 30% higher and 30% lower too, to see how sensitive the result is.
When you budget a trip, you write “petrol so much a litre, hotel so much a night”; if one gets dearer, you know which part of the budget changes.
For news with two possible outcomes (for example a deal or no deal), write out each outcome’s effect on the company separately.
A company that profits from a boom in one outcome and from a dearer dollar in the other carries less risk.
Instead of predicting the news, set up the portfolio so it stays healthy in both outcomes.
Instead of guessing whether it will rain tomorrow, you take both an umbrella and sunglasses.
A share that stays healthy either way
In summer 1405, Dr. Khosravani and Saeed Ajorlou published FIS in a scientific journal as a scoring system.
Each company is measured on 11 fundamental measures and gets a score between 0 and 100.
100 means the company got the highest score on every measure.
This lesson and the next three come from the text of that paper.
Like a report card that gives a mark for each subject and adds them up to an average; here companies get report cards.
FIS in a scientific paper
The maximum scores of the 11 measures add up to 100.
Two measures matter most, 15 points each: forward P/E (how cheap it is against this year’s profit) and sales growth.
Profit margin, margin trend, forward P/S, payout ratio, and the ratio of receivables to assets are 10 points each.
Four 5-point measures work like a quality filter: the earnings expectation gap, how fast receivables are collected, how fast goods sell, and the financial year.
Like hiring points: work experience and core skills 15 points, a few other items 10, and things like reliability 5.
The 11 measures and each one’s maximum
FIS has several steps for each measure; whichever step the measure’s value falls in, it gets that step’s fixed points.
Being slightly better earns no extra points until it reaches the next step. Total score = the sum of the 11 scores.
The paper hasn’t published the step numbers and this app doesn’t guess them. If you set steps yourself, call them “my thresholds”, not FIS.
Like karate belts: until you pass the test for the next belt, however much better you’ve got, you keep the same belt.
Stepped points
1. Loss-making companies and companies whose income can’t be predicted are set aside.
2. Each company’s 11 measures are calculated from Codal and scored.
3. Of the companies above average, the best are chosen (30 companies in the paper’s test).
4. You only buy when the price is right too. 5. With each new report, the score is recalculated.
Like picking a team: first the injured are left out, then everyone tries out, the best are picked, and every season they’re tested again.
Choosing shares in five steps
Two of the paper’s measures, how fast receivables are collected and how fast goods sell, come up a lot in his channel’s analyses too.
If a company collects its receivables faster than its own usual, that’s good; if its goods sell slower than usual, it’s a warning bell.
If debt grows 76% but shareholders’ capital only 5%, the growth came from borrowing, not profit.
He has said what shares that rose well had in common: being dividend-focused and growing net profit.
A shop whose goods sell quickly and whose credit sales are collected quickly is healthy; a shop with a warehouse full of unsold goods and debts that don’t come back isn’t.
Forward P/E = today’s price ÷ forecast earnings per share to the end of the financial year.
The forecast in the paper is simple: extend the average profit of this year’s past months to the whole year; for example 6-month profit × 2.
Forward P/S = market value ÷ forecast sales, with the same method.
The P/E tsetmc shows looks backwards; according to him we must work out profit ourselves from Codal. The “expectation gap” is the distance between these two P/Es.
If you earned 10 million a month in the first 6 months of the year, a simple estimate of the year’s income is 120 million.
Price against future profit
Sales growth: this period’s sales against the same period last year; for example this year’s 6 months against last year’s 6 months.
Profit margin: “FIS profit” divided by sales. “FIS profit” means profit without one-off and side income; a cautious view.
Margin trend: compare this quarter’s margin with last quarter’s; better or worse?
If a restaurant sold more meals this year (sales growth) and also makes more on each meal (better margin), its trend is good.
The paper defines the payout ratio in its own way: dividends paid ÷ accumulated profit (not that year’s profit), the average of the last two years.
The reason: companies sometimes pay dividends from profit left over from earlier years too.
This differs from the usual ratio (dividend ÷ earnings per share); when comparing, say which one you used.
Like asking how much of its total savings a family gives its children, not just from this year’s income.
Receivables to assets: what part of the company’s assets is money owed by customers; that is, how much it sells on credit.
Collection period: how many days it takes for sales money to arrive. Inventory turnover period: how many days it takes goods to sell.

Financial year: the paper doesn’t say exactly how it’s scored. His videos show he likes companies with different financial years so dividends arrive in different seasons, and he subtracts dividends on their way from the price.
If a shoe shop sells its stock in 30 days and gets paid in 10, its capital turns over quickly; if it takes 90 days and 60, its money is tied up.
Receivables, inventory and the financial year
Financial reports, profit and loss, and dividends come from Codal; the paper mostly used the N-10, N-30 and N-52 forms.
N-10 is usually the financial statements and N-30 the monthly report; the form code is written at the top of the announcement.
Share prices come from tsetmc.com.
According to the paper, FIS runs on just this public data and needs no complicated software.
Like cooking with ingredients from any supermarket: you don’t need to buy anything special or expensive.
Entering has two conditions: the company’s score has reached the minimum needed, and the price is right too.
Exit in two cases: the score has fallen (the company’s business or its report quality got worse), or the price has reached the target value and most of the expected return has been taken.
The portfolio shouldn’t be a single share; the number of shares depends on how many you can keep track of.
You buy good fruit when it’s both fresh and fairly priced; not cheap rotten fruit, and not good fruit at a very high price.
Good goods, the right price
In FIS the right P/E range comes from the government bond (Akhza) return plus a little for risk.
The paper’s example: if Akhza is about 40%, the buying P/E range is 3.5 to 4 and the selling range about 7 to 8.
If the Akhza return changes, these ranges change too.
Buying or selling price = target P/E × forecast earnings per share.
If the bank pays 40% a year, you’d pay at most about 350 to 400 million for a shop that makes 100 million a year, not a billion.
In Khordad 1402 all companies were scored and the 30 with the highest scores became one portfolio. The portfolio was left untouched until Khordad 1405.
Year three was a period of tension and military conflict; according to the paper the portfolio still stayed ahead of the rest.
Like a tree that gives almost no fruit in its first year and is heavy with fruit in later years; if you cut it down in year one, you lose the later years’ fruit.
The 30 portfolio shares scored between about 60 and 72. The higher the score, the higher the three-year return.
On average each extra point meant about 27.5 percentage points more return; and about three quarters of the difference in returns was explained by the score.
But this line is only for these 30 shares and this period. Outside that range it means nothing: for a score of 100 it gives more than 1,300%, which isn’t believable.
If in one class the students who studied more got better marks, you can’t say anyone who studies 20 hours a day will get a mark of 40 out of 20.
Higher score, higher return?
Shares in this same winning portfolio went, on average, about 30% below the purchase price at some point along the way.
But at their best moment they were, on average, more than 300% above the purchase price.
Anyone who sold on every fall would have missed most of the return.
On a mountain road you sometimes go down to reach the next peak; if you turn back at the first downhill, you never reach the top.
Falls and jumps along the way
427% is the nominal number. With 197% inflation over the same three years, purchasing power grew about 77%.
Over the same period, fixed-income funds cut purchasing power by about 23%.
This test is just one portfolio, one period and one starting point, and the designers ran it themselves. The score steps haven’t been published either, so others can’t repeat it yet.
The authors themselves say it must be tested in other periods too before practical use.
If your salary grows 4 times in three years but everything gets 3 times dearer, you’re really about 33% richer, not 300%.
In his 42 public videos, the exact numbers for the FIS score steps aren’t given; they’re probably in the paid course.
But for the same measures he gives benchmarks. For example: a forward P/E under 4 for buying; a P/E of 8 to 12 means “priced in”; a P/D under 5.
A payout above 60% means dividend-focused; for an FIS share, above 70%.
Read these as benchmarks, not official points.
Like a doctor who doesn’t tell you exactly how they score your health, but says “blood pressure under 12 is good”; it’s a benchmark, not the whole formula.
His ruler: the whole market’s average. The better than average, the better.
P/E, P/S and P/B: lower is better. Profit margin: 15% is average and he calls above 30% “very good”.
A higher payout, faster collection of receivables and faster-selling goods, and fewer receivables, are better.
These averages change over time and aren’t FIS score steps either.
To know whether a child is tall enough, you compare them with the average for their age, not with a fixed number.
In recent videos he says the market looks more at P/D than at P/E.
P/D = market value ÷ the year’s dividend; that is, how many years of dividends it takes for the purchase money to come back.
He sees a P/D of about 3 as ideal (the money comes back in under three years), and on his channel he writes “P/D under 5”, meaning a dividend yield of at least 20%.
If a shop costs 3 billion and pays 1 billion a year in cash rent, its P/D is 3: you get your money back in three years.
A rule he calls the “FIS indicator” in one video:
Buying price = the average of two prices: the price that makes the P/E 4 and the price that makes the P/D 4.
Selling price = the same calculation with the number 8.
It fits the paper’s example: buy at about 3.5 to 4, sell at about 7 to 8.
If earnings per share are 100 and dividend per share 80: buy at about 2 × (100 + 80) = 360, sell at about double that, 720.
His own simple rule: see how many years fixed income at today’s rate takes to return your money (1 ÷ rate), and buy the share about one unit higher.
With fixed income at about 40%, a bond returns the money in 2.5 years; so the buying P/E for a share is about 3.5 to 4.
The selling target isn’t fixed either; when interest rates are very high, he brings the target down.
As he wrote, as the Akhza rate rose, the market’s average P/E went from about 23 in 1399 to about 7 in Tir 1405.
If the bank returns your money in two and a half years at 40%, a shop that takes 10 years to return your money is expensive; about 3.5 to 4 years is sensible.
The buying P/E from the bank rate
From Shahrivar 1402 to Ordibehesht 1403, under some of his analyses, he wrote a short verdict: “valuable and attractive” or “not valuable and attractive”.
Both “attractive” ones had a P/E under 5 and all the “not” ones from 8.85 up. This is our reading of these posts, not a rule he wrote himself.
About a P/E of around 6.5 he said “right now it’s neither expensive nor attractive”, and below 5 it becomes attractive.
These are verdicts for that day at that price; they’re teaching examples, not today’s recommendations.
Like someone who has bought and sold houses for years: they take a look and say “this price is good” or “it’s expensive”; but the verdict is for that day’s price.
Instead of a price stop-loss (say “sell if it falls 10%”), he talks of a “fundamental stop-loss”: the company turning loss-making, the profit margin shrinking, or three-month sales falling.
A price swing alone isn’t a reason to sell.
An example he tells: he sold a share whose profit fell 59 to 72% and moved the money into gold.
You don’t sell a house because prices in the area dipped for a month; if its roof cracks, you do.
On his channel he has often written which share “has triggered its fundamental stop-loss” and why; for example a three-month loss, or three-month profit down 95%.
What he does after that: switch to gold, or to a share that had an excellent report.
He notes one exception: people who own a percentage of a business sometimes see the fall as temporary and wait.
These tickers are examples from old posts, not today’s recommendations.
If a tenant hasn’t paid rent for three months, you look for a better tenant; but if they’re family and you know the problem is temporary, you might wait.
The price target in his videos: a P/E or P/D of about 8, or “estimated profit × 7”.
If dividend growth falls below inflation, even in a good company, he reduces the weight rather than selling it all.
He buys and sells step by step. The “Bir rule”: when selling a share, he keeps one share of it.
Another option he gives as an example: halve a share that has doubled so your original money comes back and the other half stays “free”.
If a property you bought has doubled, you can sell half to get your money back, and keep the other half without worry.
Target price and selling in steps
His benchmark for any asset: is it ahead of gold or not?
He sees gold and silver as a safe store and changes their weight with market risk; sometimes up to half the portfolio.
In his #golden_return posts he measures shares’ returns in gold; he calls shares that are ahead of gold “more golden than gold”.
If three years ago you bought shares with the money for one gold coin and now they’re worth half a coin, you’ve fallen behind, even if the toman number has gone up.
In the paper’s test, the shares’ average biggest jump was more than 10 times their biggest fall; the authors’ conclusion: a long-term horizon and not selling early.
In his videos he says it simply: don’t touch a good share you’ve got; a few right decisions, then patience.
Patience means following the reports, not being in the dark; the fundamental stop-loss still applies.
A gardener doesn’t pull the tree out of the soil every day to see its roots; they water it, watch for pests, and wait.
The other side of the fundamental stop-loss: if the reports are good and the fundamental stop-loss hasn’t triggered, a price fall is an opportunity, not a reason to sell.
He buys in steps so that if the price falls further too, there’s still an opportunity.
Don’t measure capital in rials, measure it in real assets; the same gold ruler.
If a shop sells the same good product it always has at half price, it’s an opportunity; as long as the product really is the same.
On his channel he writes teaching analyses with a fixed template. Example: Sarbil, 6 months of 1405.
1. 6-month sales × 2 = the year’s sales “at the current pace”. 2. The year’s sales × FIS profit margin = operating profit.
3. Add recurring side income: the year’s profit.
4. Divide market value by profit, dividend and sales: forward P/E, P/D and P/S. Try this in the “FIS calculator” on the Practice tab.
If a café sold 100 million in 6 months and makes 30 tomans on every 100, at the same pace it has 200 million of sales and 60 million of profit a year.
In the same post, operating profit divided by sales comes to about 51%, but he wrote the “FIS profit margin” as 37.3%.
So “FIS profit” isn’t the reported operating profit; it’s more cautious and sets one-off items aside.
The details of these adjustments haven’t been published; if you work it out yourself as “operating profit ÷ sales”, your number will be more optimistic than his.
According to him, calculate P/E only with profit that repeats every year.
If a seller says “I make 50 million a month”, you only count the profit that repeats every month, not the month they had one exceptional order.
In the full version of the template (for example the Shifteh IPO analysis) he also adds more columns:
P/A (market value ÷ total assets) and P/B (market value ÷ shareholders’ equity); inventory turnover and collection periods; the payout percentage of the last two years.
Most of these columns are the paper’s 11 measures.
And before everything, the auditor’s report: if it was adverse or is full of problems, these numbers can’t be trusted.
Like a full car inspection form: the more columns are filled in, the fuller the picture; but if the car’s papers have a problem, the rest of the form doesn’t matter.
Next year’s dividend hasn’t been announced yet; so he estimates it: estimated profit × the average payout percentage of recent years.
The Sharanel example: with estimated profit of 7,430 billion tomans and an average payout of 90%, the forward P/D came to about 6.5.
The buying ceiling in one video: estimated profit × two-year average payout × 4.5 to 5 = the highest market value to buy at.
If a tenant pays 90% of their contract in cash every year, you estimate next year’s cash rent with the same 90%.
For holdings he has a different template; example: Saba.
Build the net asset value (NAV) yourself from the Codal portfolio report, including unlisted companies, and subtract accumulated losses.
Then he compares market value with 80% of NAV. Below 100% means the market has priced the holding at less than 80% of its assets’ value. He didn’t say why 80%.
Next to it he also gives the holding’s payout and receivables-to-assets ratio.
If a basket full of fruit is worth 1 million and they sell it for 600 thousand, it’s cheap; as long as you can really get the fruit.
Another kind of post of his: he puts an industry’s companies side by side on these same measures; for example refiners.
One has the lowest P/E, one the highest sales growth, one the highest margin, one the fewest receivables.
No company is first in every column; that’s why the FIS score weights the measures and adds them up.
He also compares margins only within one industry.
When buying a phone, one has a better camera, one a better battery, one is cheaper; you give each feature a weight and add them up.
He judges IPOs like any other share: the offer price against the per-share value in the pricing report, and the profit forecast.
For example an offering that, according to his post, was “25% below the calculated value”.
The FIS question is the same: at the offer price, what are the forward P/E and dividend yield? Do the three golden conditions hold?
A new-build house is still a house; the “new-build” label is no reason not to check its size, price and area.
If the company’s 6-month profit has already reached a large part of the whole year’s forecast, the forecast was cautious.
The channel’s example: 6-month profit had reached about 97% of the whole year’s estimate.

All of FIS in seven steps (we arranged the order; every step comes from his paper, videos or channel):
1. Readiness: 3 to 7-year money, below your capacity, no loans; on his advice 6 to 12 months of learning first. 2. Screen: loss-making and weak companies are set aside.
3. The three golden conditions. 4. Estimate profit to year-end from Codal. 5. P/E, P/S, P/D and benchmarks better than the market average.
6. The right price (from the Akhza rate and a P/D under 5), buying in steps. 7. Monitor every report; sell on the fundamental stop-loss or on reaching the target; compare with gold.
Like buying a rental property: money ready, cut the bad options, check the rent, work out the year’s income, compare with others, haggle on price, and then check in regularly.

The year’s sales = sales of the reported months ÷ number of months × 12 (“at the current pace”).
Profit = the year’s sales × FIS profit margin (without one-off items) + recurring side income.
Work with the parent company’s report, not the consolidated one. The EPS and P/E on tsetmc look backwards; build the forward number yourself.
If last year’s meeting hasn’t been held yet, subtract the dividend on its way from the market value. He sets aside businesses with unpredictable sales.
You work out a taxi’s yearly income from its last few months, with its usual takings; not from the day a passenger gave a big tip.

When buying a used car, you don’t even look at a flood-damaged car or one without papers, however cheap it is.
The price ceiling can be worked out three ways:
1. From P/E: estimated profit × buying P/E (which comes from the Akhza rate; in one video 4 to 4.5).
2. From P/D: estimated profit × average payout × 4.5 to 5. 3. From return: if a share’s expected return is below the interest rate (about 40% at the time), he goes to gold.
All three say the same thing: a share must give more than fixed income. And buying is in steps.
To know the most you’d pay for a shop, you look at its profit, its cash rent, and what the bank would give you for the same money.
Fundamental stop-loss: a loss, a falling quarterly margin, or falling sales. After that: gold or a share with a better report.
Target: a P/E or P/D of about 7 to 8; for a holding, up to NAV.
If dividend growth falls below inflation, reduce the weight; don’t sell it all.
